summary: Rand's view of what standards computer service centers on the network should follow, written as input for a panel discussion at the October 1971 meeting. It argues that common appearance and behavior across service centers would help users, and that service centers must follow the official network protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC argues that common procedures and clear information would help people use remote computer service centers. It lists areas to standardize or document, from job entry and login to costs and support.

questions: what service center standards did rfc 231 propose
subtitle: A user's view of common procedures for ARPANET service centers.

tldr.problem: Different service centers present different procedures and information to remote users, making it harder to use several sites.
tldr.mechanism: The authors identify areas where common appearance, operation or documentation could help users and resource-access programs.
tldr.outcome: The note proposes a service-center standards manual or notebook and offers its views for a panel discussion.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 231 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The document presents the authors' views for a service-center discussion.

sections.title: Why Service Centers Need Common Rules
sections.content:
The note presents the authors' views for a service-center panel discussion. It assumes that service centers will follow official network protocols, because their practices affect other parts of the network and minimal hosts such as TIPs.

Common service appearance and behavior could help users and the people building resource-access programs. The authors focus on external performance, operations and procedure documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote users should not have to learn a completely different way to reach every service center. Common procedures can also let one access program work with more than one service.

sections.title: Areas to Standardize
sections.content:
The note identifies remote job entry as one area: the UCSB and UCLA facilities used different data protocols, so a common interface could let users select a service without learning its site's details. It also discusses login, subsystem access and a common way to describe charges that use storage, I/O, connection time and CPU resources.

Other areas include off-line services, job scheduling, priorities, status information, documentation, operating schedules, consulting and procedures for failures. Consistent information could help users compare sites while allowing the services themselves to differ.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal covers how users log in, submit jobs, understand charges and get help. It also suggests publishing operating schedules and status information in a consistent format.

sections.title: Documentation for Users
sections.content:
The authors suggest expanding the Resource Notebook or creating a separate service-center standards notebook. Some information should use a common format even when the service itself cannot be made uniform, such as operating hours or local storage policies.

The summary calls for a manual of service-center standards and documentation about the services available. It also says some sites may offer special resources without being able or willing to meet the proposed standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared guide could explain how each center works and what it offers. The services can still differ, as long as users can find comparable information about them.
